title: Control Flow: if, for, switch
summary: Control flow is how a program decides **what to do next**. Go keeps it deliberately small: `if` for branching (no parentheses, braces always required), `for` as the **only** loop keyword, and `switch` for clean multi-way choices that don't fall through by default.

subtopics.title: if and if-with-init
subtopics.explanation: Conditions have no parentheses but braces are mandatory. An optional init statement runs first and scopes its variables to the if/else: `if err := f(); err != nil { ... }`. This keeps short-lived variables out of the surrounding scope. Within Control Flow: if, for, switch, `if` is Go's fundamental branching construct.

subtopics.title: for is Go's only loop
subtopics.explanation: There is no `while` or `do`. The three-component for is `for init; cond; post {}`; drop the init and post for a while-style `for cond {}`; drop everything for an infinite `for {}`. As part of Control Flow: if, for, switch, `for` is the single keyword that expresses every kind of iteration in Go.

subtopics.title: for-range
subtopics.explanation: Iterate slices, arrays, maps, strings, and channels. Over a slice you get index and value; over a map, key and value; over a string you get the byte index and a rune (not a byte). Use _ to discard either side. In Control Flow: if, for, switch, `for-range` is the idiomatic form of the `for` loop for walking collections.

subtopics.title: break, continue, and labels
subtopics.explanation: break exits the innermost loop or switch; continue skips to the next iteration. A label lets you break or continue an outer loop from inside a nested one: `break Outer`. These keywords give you fine-grained control over the flow inside Go's loops within Control Flow: if, for, switch.

subtopics.title: switch without fallthrough
subtopics.explanation: Cases do NOT fall through by default, so you never write `break`. One case can match multiple values (comma-separated). Use the explicit `fallthrough` keyword on the rare occasion you want the next case to also run. This safe-by-default behavior is a defining feature of `switch` within Control Flow: if, for, switch.

subtopics.title: Expressionless switch and type switch
subtopics.explanation: A switch with no expression evaluates `true`, acting as a clean if/else-if chain. A type switch — `switch v := x.(type)` — branches on the dynamic type stored in an interface value. Both forms extend `switch` beyond simple value matching, rounding out the tools of Control Flow: if, for, switch.

foundations.overview: Every program has to choose between paths and repeat work, and Go gives you exactly three constructs for it: `if`, `for`, and `switch`. The design philosophy is minimalism — there is no `while`, no `do-while`, and no ternary operator. Instead, `for` flexes into all looping shapes, `if` supports a tidy init statement, and `switch` replaces long if/else chains while avoiding C's accidental fall-through. Master these three and you can express any control flow idiomatically.
foundations.formalDefinition: Control flow statements determine the order in which statements execute. Go provides conditional branching (`if`/`else`), iteration (`for`, the sole loop keyword, including the `range` form), and multi-way selection (`switch`, including expressionless and type switches), augmented by `break`, `continue`, and labels.
foundations.whyItMatters: Control flow is the skeleton of every function you write. Go's specific rules — mandatory braces, the if-with-init idiom for error handling, no default fall-through, and a single loop keyword — show up in essentially every Go file and in nearly every beginner interview.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a railway junction. `if` is a switch that sends the train down one of two tracks based on a signal. `for` is a loop of track the train circles until a gate opens. `switch` is a multi-platform station that routes the train to exactly one platform — and unlike a leaky station, it never lets the train drift onto the next platform unless you explicitly say `fallthrough`.
commonUseCases: Iterating slices, maps, and strings with for-range
Dispatching on value or dynamic type with switch

commonMisconceptions.reality: It doesn't. A condition-only `for cond {}` is the while loop, and a bare `for {}` is the infinite loop.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You need `break` at the end of each switch case.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go cases don't fall through, so `break` is unnecessary; use the explicit `fallthrough` keyword on the rare occasion you actually want it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Ranging over a string gives you bytes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It yields the starting byte index and the decoded rune (Unicode code point); index a string directly (`s[i]`) to get a byte.

commonMisconceptions.myth: if conditions need parentheses like C.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go forbids the parentheses but requires the braces, even for a one-line body.

visualExplorer.title: How a three-component for loop executes
visualExplorer.caption: The init, condition, and post parts run in a fixed order; the body runs only when the condition is true.

config.intro: Execution order of `for init; cond; post { body }`:

steps.name: Run init once
steps.detail: The init statement (e.g. `i := 0`) executes a single time before the loop and scopes its variables to the loop.

steps.name: Check condition
steps.detail: The condition (e.g. `i < n`) is evaluated. If false, the loop ends immediately and control jumps past it.

steps.name: Execute body
steps.detail: If the condition was true, the loop body runs once.

steps.name: Run post
steps.detail: After the body, the post statement (e.g. `i++`) executes.

steps.name: Loop back
steps.detail: Control returns to the condition check, repeating body+post until the condition is false.

visualExplorer.title: How a switch is evaluated
visualExplorer.caption: Go compares the switch value against each case in order, runs the first match, and stops — no fall-through.

config.intro: Evaluating `switch x { case a: ...; case b, c: ...; default: ... }`:

steps.name: Evaluate the switch value
steps.detail: `x` is computed once (or `true` is used if the switch has no expression).

steps.name: Compare cases top to bottom
steps.detail: Each case expression is compared to `x` in source order; a comma-separated case matches if ANY of its values match.

steps.name: Run the first matching case
steps.detail: The matched case's body runs. There is no implicit `break` needed and no fall-through to the next case.

steps.name: fallthrough (optional)
steps.detail: If the case ends with the `fallthrough` keyword, control transfers into the NEXT case's body unconditionally.

steps.name: default if nothing matched
steps.detail: If no case matched, the `default` case (if present) runs; otherwise the switch does nothing.

interactiveExamples.title: The four shapes of for
interactiveExamples.explanation: Go has one loop keyword. Here it appears as a classic counter loop, a while-style condition loop, an infinite loop with break, and a range loop — all using `for`.

interactiveExamples.title: if-with-init and a clean switch
interactiveExamples.explanation: The if-with-init form scopes `ok` to the if/else only. The switch needs no break statements and uses a comma-separated case to group weekend days.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: range over a string correctly
interactiveExamples.explanation: Indexing a string gives a byte; ranging gives runes. This snippet should print each character (rune) of a string that contains a non-ASCII letter. Fix the loop so it prints runes, not raw bytes.

checkpoints.code:
n := 7
switch {
case n < 5:
	fmt.Println("small")
case n < 10:
	fmt.Println("medium")
default:
	fmt.Println("large")
}
checkpoints.explanation: An expressionless switch evaluates `true` and runs the first case whose condition is true. `n < 5` is false, `n < 10` is true, so it prints "medium" and stops — there is no fall-through to default.

checkpoints.prompt: This is meant to break out of BOTH loops when it finds a match. What's wrong?
options: break is not allowed inside range loops
Plain break only exits the inner loop; the outer loop keeps going
checkpoints.explanation: An unlabeled break exits only the innermost loop, so the outer loop continues scanning. Use a label: put `Search:` before the outer `for` and write `break Search` to exit both at once.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does idiomatic Go often write `if err := doThing(); err != nil { ... }`?
options: It runs doThing twice for safety
The init statement scopes err to the if/else, keeping it out of the surrounding function
It is required syntax for error handling
checkpoints.explanation: The optional init statement runs once and limits the lifetime of `err` to the if/else block, avoiding an unused or leaked variable in the enclosing scope. It is a convention, not a requirement.

checkpoints.prompt: Make this loop run forever until an internal condition breaks it (an event/worker loop).
checkpoints.explanation: A bare `for {}` (nothing between `for` and the brace) is Go's infinite loop. The other forms are not valid Go for an unconditional loop; you simply omit all three components.

codeLab.title: FizzBuzz with for + switch
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Solve(n int) []string` that returns the FizzBuzz result for 1..n: "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for multiples of 5, "FizzBuzz" for multiples of 15, and the number as a string otherwise. Use a for loop and an expressionless switch.

solution.code:
package solution

import "strconv"

func Solve(n int) []string {
	out := make([]string, 0, n) // pre-size to n results
	for i := 1; i <= n; i++ {
		switch { // expressionless switch == if/else-if chain
		case i%15 == 0: // check 15 first; it implies both 3 and 5
			out = append(out, "FizzBuzz")
		case i%3 == 0:
			out = append(out, "Fizz")
		case i%5 == 0:
			out = append(out, "Buzz")
		default:
			out = append(out, strconv.Itoa(i))
		}
	}
	return out
}

hints: Loop with `for i := 1; i <= n; i++` so you cover 1 through n inclusive.
Use an expressionless `switch { case ... }` and check the multiple-of-15 case FIRST.
Convert the plain number with strconv.Itoa(i) in the default case.

debuggingLab.title: Ported C switch runs the wrong cases
debuggingLab.symptom: A developer coming from C added `break` and expected only one case to run, but is surprised the program already worked without it — and worse, after adding `fallthrough` to 'be safe', extra cases now execute.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: In Go, switch cases do not fall through by default, so `break` is never needed to separate them. The `fallthrough` keyword here is both unreachable (it sits after a `return`) and reflects a C habit. When `fallthrough` IS reachable, it transfers control into the next case's body unconditionally without testing that case's value — almost never the intended behavior.
commonMistakes: Adding `break` at the end of each case (harmless but unnecessary noise).
Adding `fallthrough` thinking it is required, causing the next case to run unexpectedly.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Remove the stray `fallthrough` so each case stands alone, which is Go's default behavior.

solution.expectedOutput:
label(1) -> one
label(2) -> two
label(9) -> other

theory.question: Go has no `while` keyword. How do you write a while loop and an infinite loop?
theory.directAnswer: Use `for`, Go's only loop keyword. A while loop is a condition-only `for cond { ... }`; an infinite loop is a bare `for { ... }` with no init, condition, or post. You exit either with `break` (or `return`).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The `for` statement has three optional parts (init; condition; post). Omitting parts yields the while and infinite forms.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go's designers chose one flexible loop construct over several keywords to keep the language small and uniform.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: `for cond {}` evaluates cond before each iteration and stops when it is false; `for {}` has no condition and loops until a break/return.

theory.whyImportant: It is a near-universal first question about Go control flow and trips up developers from C-family languages.
theory.realWorldExample: A worker loop `for { job := <-jobs; process(job) }` runs until the channel is closed and the loop breaks.

followUps.question: How do you write a do-while (run the body at least once)?
followUps.answer: Use a `for {}` with the exit condition checked at the bottom: run the body, then `if done { break }`.

followUps.question: Can a for loop have just a post statement?
followUps.answer: You can omit any of the three parts; typically you keep at least the condition or use a bare loop, but each component is independently optional.

theory.question: How does Go's switch differ from C's, and what is `fallthrough`?
theory.directAnswer: Go's switch does not fall through between cases by default, so you never write `break` to separate them — the first matching case runs and the switch exits. A case can list multiple comma-separated values. If you explicitly want the next case to also execute, you end a case with the `fallthrough` keyword, which jumps into the next case's body unconditionally.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A multi-way branch that compares a value (or `true`, when expressionless) against case expressions in order.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: C's implicit fall-through caused a notorious class of bugs from forgotten `break`s; Go inverts the default to be safe and adds `fallthrough` for the rare opposite need.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Cases are tested top to bottom; the first match runs and the switch ends. `fallthrough` overrides that to enter the next case without testing its condition.

theory.whyImportant: Misunderstanding fall-through is a classic source of bugs and a frequent interview probe for C-to-Go converts.
theory.realWorldExample: Mapping an HTTP status class with `case 200, 201, 204: return "success"` groups multiple values cleanly in one case.

followUps.question: What is an expressionless switch?
followUps.answer: A `switch { case cond: ... }` with no value after `switch`; it implicitly compares against `true`, making a clean if/else-if chain.

followUps.question: Does fallthrough re-evaluate the next case's condition?
followUps.answer: No. It enters the next case's body unconditionally, regardless of whether that case would have matched.

theory.question: What does ranging over a string give you, and how is it different from indexing with s[i]?
theory.directAnswer: `for i, r := range s` yields the starting byte index i and the decoded rune r (a Unicode code point) for each character, correctly decoding multi-byte UTF-8. Indexing with s[i] instead gives a single byte (uint8), so for non-ASCII characters it returns only one fragment of a multi-byte sequence. Range is the right tool when you care about characters; indexing is for raw bytes.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to walk a string: rune-by-rune with range, or byte-by-byte with indexing.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go strings are UTF-8 byte sequences; range provides a convenient character-level view while s[i] exposes the underlying bytes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: range advances by the byte-width of each rune (so indices may skip), decoding each code point; s[i] simply reads the byte at offset i and len(s) counts bytes, not characters.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing bytes and runes causes garbled output and off-by-one bugs with any non-ASCII text — a very common interview and code-review topic.
theory.realWorldExample: Counting characters in a username like 'héllo' — range reports 5 runes, while len('héllo') is 6 bytes because é is two bytes.

followUps.question: Why did the byte index jump from 1 to 3 in the 'héllo' example?
followUps.answer: The é occupies two bytes (indices 1 and 2), so the next rune 'l' starts at byte index 3.

followUps.question: How do you get the number of characters (runes) in a string?
followUps.answer: Use utf8.RuneCountInString(s), or convert to []rune and take len; len(s) alone counts bytes.

theory.question: What is an expressionless switch, and when would you use it over an if/else-if chain?
theory.directAnswer: An expressionless switch is `switch { case cond1: ...; case cond2: ...; default: ... }` with no value after the switch keyword. Go implicitly compares each case against `true`, so it behaves exactly like an if/else-if chain, running the first case whose boolean condition is true. It's preferred when you have three or more mutually exclusive boolean branches because it reads more cleanly and groups the alternatives visually.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A switch with no switch expression, where each case is a boolean condition.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It gives a tidy, aligned syntax for multi-way boolean branching without repeating `else if` and without a ternary operator (which Go lacks).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The omitted expression defaults to the constant true; cases are evaluated top to bottom and the first true condition's body runs, then the switch exits (no fall-through).

theory.whyImportant: It's an idiomatic Go pattern (used in the FizzBuzz-style classification) and interviewers often ask candidates to convert an if/else-if ladder into it.
theory.realWorldExample: Classifying an HTTP status code: `switch { case code < 300: ...; case code < 400: ...; default: ... }` reads better than nested if/else.

followUps.question: Does order matter in an expressionless switch?
followUps.answer: Yes — cases are checked top to bottom and only the first true one runs, so put more specific conditions first (e.g. i%15 before i%3).

followUps.question: Can you still use an init statement with an expressionless switch?
followUps.answer: Yes: `switch x := f(); { case x > 0: ... }` scopes x to the switch just like if-with-init.

scenario.question: You're searching a 2D grid in nested loops and need to stop both loops the moment you find a match, then run code after them. A flag-based approach is getting messy. What's the idiomatic fix?
scenario.directAnswer: Use a labeled break. Put a label before the outer loop and `break Label` from inside the inner loop to exit both at once, without flags. If you instead wanted to skip to the next outer iteration, use `continue Label`. If finding the value should end the whole function, an early `return` is even cleaner.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Labels are identifiers placed before a loop that `break`/`continue` can target to control an outer loop.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An unlabeled break only exits the innermost loop, so labels provide structured multi-level exit without `goto` or boolean flags.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: `break Outer` transfers control to just after the loop labeled `Outer`; `continue Outer` jumps to that loop's next iteration.

scenario.whyImportant: Nested-loop control comes up in grid/graph problems and in real parsers; the labeled-break idiom is the clean Go answer.
scenario.realWorldExample: Scanning a matrix for a sentinel value and breaking out of both loops to report the coordinates.

followUps.question: When would you prefer extracting a function with `return` over a labeled break?
followUps.answer: When the search naturally yields a result; a helper that returns on match is often clearer than labels and keeps the caller flat.

scenario.question: A colleague ported a C validation function to Go and left `break` at the end of every switch case. It works, but a reviewer asks them to remove the breaks. Are the breaks harmful, and what's the deeper risk in porting C switches?
scenario.directAnswer: The trailing `break`s are harmless but redundant noise — Go cases don't fall through, so each case already stops on its own. The real risk in porting from C is the opposite direction: a C developer who forgets that Go doesn't fall through may either add `fallthrough` unnecessarily (causing the next case to run unexpectedly) or, in C, forget a break and get accidental fall-through. Remove the redundant breaks for idiomatic Go, and only add `fallthrough` where the next case must deliberately also run.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The behavioral difference between C's fall-through-by-default switch and Go's stop-by-default switch.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go inverts C's default because forgotten breaks were a notorious C bug class; the safe default is no fall-through.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: In Go the first matching case runs and control exits the switch automatically; `break` is only needed to leave a case early, and `fallthrough` is the explicit opt-in to enter the next case.

scenario.whyImportant: Mismatched fall-through assumptions are a real source of logic bugs during C-to-Go migrations and a favorite interview probe.
scenario.realWorldExample: Porting a state-machine dispatch: removing stray breaks and only keeping the one intentional fallthrough where two adjacent states share setup logic.

followUps.question: Where can `break` legitimately appear inside a switch case?
followUps.answer: To exit the switch early before the case body finishes, or to break out of a loop that encloses the switch (with a label if needed).

followUps.question: Is `break` inside a switch the same as `break` inside a loop?
followUps.answer: An unlabeled break exits the innermost switch OR loop that contains it; inside a switch it exits the switch, so use a label to break an enclosing loop from within a switch.

systemDesign.question: You're designing a long-running background worker that pulls jobs from a queue until shutdown. How would you structure its main loop and dispatch logic using Go's control-flow constructs?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Use a bare `for {}` as the event loop and a `switch` (often a type switch or a select-like dispatch) to route each job. Inside the loop, read the next job, use an if-with-init to handle read/decode errors early, `continue` to skip a bad job, and `break` (or return) to exit on a shutdown signal. A `switch job.Type { ... }` dispatches to the right handler with no fall-through, and comma-separated cases group related job types.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A worker loop combining Go's only loop keyword with switch-based dispatch and break/continue for flow control.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Servers and workers are fundamentally infinite loops that process events until told to stop; Go's for/switch/if cover this cleanly without extra keywords.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: `for {}` loops forever; each iteration fetches a job, if-with-init guards errors, switch dispatches by type, `continue` skips, and a shutdown condition triggers `break`/`return` to end the loop.

systemDesign.whyImportant: The infinite-loop + dispatch pattern underlies almost every Go service, consumer, and daemon, exercising every control-flow construct in this topic.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A message-queue consumer: `for { job, ok := <-jobs; if !ok { break }; switch job.Kind { case Email, SMS: ...; case Report: ...; default: log } }`.

followUps.question: How would you add graceful shutdown to this loop?
followUps.answer: Use `select` over the jobs channel and a done/context channel; when the done channel fires, `return` to exit the loop cleanly.

followUps.question: Why prefer a bare `for {}` over `for true {}`?
followUps.answer: They compile to the same thing, but `for {}` is the idiomatic Go infinite loop; `for true {}` is redundant and non-idiomatic.

coding.question: Implement `func Describe(x interface{}) string` that returns a label for the dynamic type of x: "int", "string", "bool", or "unknown". Use a type switch.
coding.thoughtProcess: A value stored in an empty interface carries its dynamic type. A type switch — `switch v := x.(type)` — branches on that type and binds `v` to the concrete value in each case, letting us return a label per type and fall back to a default for anything else.

solution.code:
func Describe(x interface{}) string {
	switch v := x.(type) { // v is typed per case
	case int:
		_ = v // v is an int here
		return "int"
	case string:
		return "string"
	case bool:
		return "bool"
	default:
		return "unknown"
	}
}

coding.lineByLine: `x.(type)` is only valid inside a switch; each case names a concrete type, and `v` takes that type within the case body. `case int` matches when x's dynamic type is int, and so on. The `default` handles any other type (including nil), returning "unknown".
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — a fixed number of type comparisons.

followUps.question: What does `v` equal in the default case?
followUps.answer: It keeps the original interface type (interface{}), holding whatever value x had, since no specific case matched.

followUps.question: How would you handle multiple types in one branch?
followUps.answer: List them comma-separated, e.g. `case int, int64:` — but then `v` keeps the interface type since the cases differ.

coding.question: Implement `func CountVowels(s string) int` that counts the vowels (a, e, i, o, u, case-insensitive) in s. Use for-range over the string and a switch.
coding.thoughtProcess: Ranging over a string yields runes, which correctly handles multi-byte characters. For each rune we lowercase it (add 32 only for A-Z, or use unicode.ToLower) and use an expressionless-style switch with comma-separated case values to match any vowel. A matching case increments the counter; the default does nothing.
coding.lineByLine: We range over s so each r is a decoded rune. unicode.ToLower(r) normalizes uppercase vowels to lowercase so we only list five cases. The switch has one case with five comma-separated values; matching any of them runs the body and increments count. There is no fallthrough and no default is needed since non-vowels are simply ignored.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) where n is the number of runes in s.

followUps.question: Why range over the string instead of indexing with s[i]?
followUps.answer: s[i] yields a byte, which mishandles multi-byte UTF-8 characters; range decodes proper runes so accented or non-ASCII text works correctly.

followUps.question: Could you use an expressionless switch instead?
followUps.answer: Yes — `switch { case r == 'a' || r == 'e' || ...: }` works, but the value switch with comma-separated cases is cleaner here.

keyTakeaways: `if` takes no parentheses but always requires braces, and its optional init statement (`if v, ok := f(); ok {}`) scopes variables to the if/else.
`for` is Go's only loop: three-component, condition-only (while), bare infinite, and the `range` form — use labels with break/continue to control nested loops.
for-range over a string yields a byte index and a rune; over slices it yields index+value and over maps key+value.
switch cases do NOT fall through (no `break` needed), can match multiple comma-separated values, support an expressionless if/else-if form, and a type switch (`x.(type)`) branches on dynamic type.
